1:
Paul left Athens unpersecuted, which is itself a comment. Henry notes he was not driven out, as he was from every place where the Jews had interest enough to raise a mob; the reception was simply cold, with "little prospect of doing good there", so he left the believers to Dionysius and went on. Wesley is blunter about why nothing took: "The philosophers there were too easy, too indolent, and too wise in their own eyes to receive the Gospel."

Corinth was the opposite city in every respect. Barnes calls it "the Paris of antiquity; the seat of splendour, and show, and corruption", where lasciviousness "was not only practised and allowed, but was consecrated by the worship of Venus", so that the temple offerings of licentious passion funded the city's magnificence. Robertson puts the same point in numbers — a thousand consecrated prostitutes at the Aphrodite temple on the Acrocorinthus, and a verb, to Corinthianize, that simply meant immorality. His summary of the change of scene is exact: "Not the Parthenon with Athene faced Paul in Corinth, but a worse situation."

The historical notes converge. Mummius destroyed the city in 146 B.C.; Julius Caesar refounded it as a colony; it recovered its splendour and its vices together. Barnes adds that in the conflagration fused metals ran together to make Corinthian brass, Clarke that the Corinthian order of architecture began there, and Robertson that the two ports and the ship-hauling isthmus gave it command of the trade between Asia and Rome. Clarke records the city reduced, in his own century, to some thirteen thousand souls.

Calvin refuses to let the improbability pass. Paul enters this rich and crowded place "a simple man, unknown, having no eloquence or pomp, showing no wealth or power" — and the gulf does not swallow him. That it did not is the argument: such a result from such means proves the Spirit's power rather than any human cause, and lets Paul call the Corinthians the seal of his apostleship (1 Corinthians 9:2). "They be twice blind, who do not acknowledge that the glory of God did more plainly appear in such a simple and base kind of dealing."

On Aquila himself the voices divide. Gill takes trouble to keep him distinct from the two men he is often confused with — the proselyte Aquila who made the Greek version, and Onkelos the Chaldee paraphrast — arguing that neither name nor nation fits. Clarke goes the other way and thinks Onkelos may be the very man. Robertson notes only that the translator was also from Pontus and leaves the coincidence alone.

Whether the couple were already Christians is disputed on the same silence. Barnes says it is evident Aquila became a convert; Clarke insists "we have no evidence that this Jew and his wife were at this time converted", and makes their conversion the fruit of Paul's lodging with them; Robertson reads Luke's bare "a Jew" as meaning "apparently not yet a disciple". How Paul found them nobody knows, though Robertson cites Edersheim on trade guilds keeping together in street and synagogue.

Claudius's edict is unrecorded by Josephus and known from Suetonius, who says the Jews were expelled for "constantly exciting tumults under their leader, Chrestus". Barnes builds five steps to the conclusion that a Roman historian mistook Christ for a living ringleader; Robertson agrees, dating it about A.D. 49. Clarke will not have it: "how could he intend Christ, who was never at Rome?" Chrestus, he insists, "is no fictitious name, no name of an absent person, nor of a sect", but a real agitator who suffered for it. Calvin sees past the politics to the providence — Paul's only host in Corinth was a man twice exiled, and "this happy calamity of Aquila doth teach us, that the Lord doth often better provide for us when he doth sharply punish us."
3:
That an educated Pharisee had a trade in his hands surprises nobody here, because it was the rule. Robertson quotes Rabbi Judah — "He that teacheth not his son a trade, doth the same as if he taught him to be a thief" — and Barnes adds Maimonides, that "the wise generally practise some of the arts, lest they should be dependent on the charity of others." Wesley turns the custom into a rebuke: it was a rule among the Jews "(and why is it not among the Christians?) to bring up all their children to some trade, were they ever so rich or noble."

What the trade actually was, nobody can say. Barnes reports that many made the word a weaver of tapestry, as Luther translated it, but prefers a maker of tents from skin or cloth; Robertson specifies leather or goat's-hair cloth. Clarke canvasses the field — skin tents for soldiers and travellers, linen ones, theatre hangings, even "a sort of umbrella-maker" — then gives up honestly: "In short, we know not what the trade was. I have generally preferred the notion of a carpenter." Calvin defends the ancient report that Paul was a leatherworker as no contradiction of Luke, "because they were wont at that time to make tents of skins."

Why he worked divides the two temperaments. Barnes reads plain necessity: "it seems pretty evident that it was because he had no other means of maintenance." Calvin reads strategy — the false apostles taught without charge so as to "craftily creep in", and Paul refused to concede them that advantage (1 Corinthians 9:12). Clarke's interest is the modern application, pressed hard: why should a man who knows the way of salvation not explain it to his neighbours because he is a tent-maker? "How many of the clergy, and other ministers, are farmers, graziers, schoolmasters, and sleeping partners in different trades and commercial concerns! A tent-maker, in his place, is as useful as any of these."

Gill draws the weekly rhythm from the two verses: the sabbath in the synagogue, the weekdays at the bench. He also records the Latin addition "interposing the name of the Lord Jesus", which Calvin dismisses — "it is a wonder how that crept in", supplied by "some reader" wanting the sentence completed. Calvin's own reading of the method is that Paul began indirectly, because the Jews handled the law coldly, opening instead on corrupt nature, the necessity of grace and the promised Redeemer as "a fit and brief preparation unto Christ", naming Christ plainly only later. Teachers should therefore "wisely consider where to begin, lest a preposterous and confused order do hinder the proceeding of doctrine."

Then a textual fork. Was Paul pressed in spirit or constrained by the word? Clarke lays out the manuscripts, notes that Griesbach took the second into the text, and declares "there can be no doubt" of it; Ellicott agrees the better copies read "constrained by the Word", the Word within him "as a constraining power"; Robertson accepts the reading but breaks with the translators over the voice, making the verb a direct middle — Paul held himself wholly to preaching, no longer only on sabbaths. Barnes and Wesley keep the older text and read an inward impulse, Wesley urging every Christian to watch for such pressure and follow it if it agrees with Scripture.

What changed him is disputed too. Robertson credits the Macedonian gifts, which released him from the bench for a season; Ellicott flatly refuses that — "there is no indication of his giving up tent-making" — and suggests instead that meeting people lately from Rome rekindled a desire he had nursed for years (Romans 15:23). Wesley thinks simply that the news the two men brought did it. Clarke ends on a quieter note: after this verse Silas vanishes from the record, and "probably he died in Macedonia."
6:
The verb behind "opposed themselves" is military. Clarke reads "systematically opposing, putting themselves in warlike order against him", Robertson a ranging in battle array face to face. Calvin watches the sequence instead: they move from gainsaying to blaspheming, the ordinary progress — "when men take to themselves such liberty, that the devil doth inflame them by little and little unto greater madness." Clarke does not stop at Corinth but turns the verse into a standing charge against the Jews of his own century — his polemic, not Luke's.

Shaking the raiment is read as prophetic sign rather than temper. Clarke supplies Nehemiah 5:13 — "so shall God shake every man from his house and from his labour" — and takes Paul to be under a divine impulse, foreshadowing a dispersion "about sixteen years afterwards". Barnes gives it two senses, disowning their guilt and predicting their rejection. Ellicott, alert to who does it to whom, calls it the one act by which a Jew could so protest to Jews, "the last resource of one who found appeals to reason and conscience powerless". Robertson borrows Ramsay: "undoubtedly a very exasperating gesture."

"Your blood be upon your own heads" is not a curse, Robertson insists, citing Page — it is "a solemn disclaimer of responsibility", and the very phrase the Jews had used of Christ's blood (Matthew 27:25). Ellicott and Calvin both hear Ezekiel 3:18 behind it, and Calvin turns it on the ministry: since God said "I will require his blood at thy hand", teachers must "do what in them lieth to bring those which go astray into the way."

How far the turn to the Gentiles reaches is genuinely contested. Ellicott says the words "have a limited and local application" — Paul gave up the Corinthian synagogue, not the nation, and Wesley agrees: "Only he preached no more in their synagogue." Robertson calls Corinth the turning point yet notes Paul preaching to Jews later at Ephesus and Rome. Calvin alone reads it nationally, as an inheritance transferred to the Gentiles to shame Israel into repentance — though, being incurable, they got only despair from it.

Whether Paul moved house splits them cleanly. Clarke has him leave his lodging and go "to lodge with Justus"; Henry denies it — "not to lodge, for he continued with Aquila and Priscilla, but to preach" — and Wesley and Calvin agree, Calvin adding that the move was not weariness of his hosts but a way to come nearer the Gentiles. The better manuscripts prefix Titus; Ellicott weighs whether this is the Titus of the epistles and refuses to decide, while Robertson decides briskly that he is not, the Titii being a famous family of Corinthian potters.

The house adjoined the synagogue, and the reason offered depends on the reader. Henry suspects some will call it poaching but prefers charity: Paul "would come as near to them as he could", ready to return if received. Calvin proposes the opposite motive outright — Paul chose that house "that he might the more nettle the Jews". Robertson declines both: "whether Paul chose this location for his work because it was next to the synagogue, we do not know, but it caught the attendants at the synagogue worship." The lines, he adds, were drawn by the Jews themselves.

Then the synagogue lost its ruler. Clarke lists what the office carried — presiding, interpreting the law, excommunicating, marrying, divorcing — so the defection was galling; he supposes Sosthenes filled the seat. Ellicott notes Paul broke his own habit to baptize so conspicuous a convert himself (1 Corinthians 1:14); Calvin, seeing Sosthenes bear the same title soon after, infers Crispus was one chief man among several, not the sole head. Robertson's summary: "It looked like ruin for the synagogue." Barnes draws the wider inference — if a church could stand in Corinth, no city is beyond it.
9:
The vision comes because Paul is afraid, and every voice says so. Barnes guesses at the fear — the learning and splendour of the city, the awkwardness of addressing the rich and polite — and cites Paul's own account of himself there, "in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling" (1 Corinthians 2:3). Ellicott adds the social sting: his converts came mostly from the slave and freedman class, while his cultural equals held back. Robertson finds the same dejection in a letter written just then (2 Thessalonians 3:2) and refuses to make it exotic — "every pastor knows what it is to have such moods and moments." Both he and Ellicott reach independently for Elijah and Jeremiah.

Whether it was a dream is disputed in passing. Gill says Christ appeared to him asleep, in a dream. Calvin will not allow the word, since Scripture distinguishes visions from dreams (Numbers 12:6): Paul was in a trance and "saw a certain shape or form whereby he knew that God was present with him."

Robertson presses the tenses: "stop being afraid, but go on speaking and do not become silent" — the fear already present, the silence not yet begun. Calvin draws a rule from the pairing. Fear does not merely stop the mouth; it makes men speak guardedly, so the command adds hold not thy peace: "speak not with half thy mouth, as it is in the common proverb." Ministers must keep back nothing that edifies, since "nothing is more contrary to the pure and free preaching of the gospel than the straits of a faint heart."

"I am with thee" raises Calvin's sharpest question: had Paul not this already, the promise being general (Matthew 28:20)? His answer is that God applies the general word to particular cases as they require it; Ellicott and Robertson say the same more gently — the promise to the Church "received a personal application". Calvin then qualifies the protection carefully: it does not mean Paul will be spared violence, for the Jews assaulted him afterwards, but that "their attempts shall be frustrate". Clarke reads a plot behind it — "no man shall be permitted to lay violent hands upon thee."

The crux is "I have much people in this city", and it divides the corpus five ways. Barnes takes it as proof of a fixed decree — "there is no chance; no hap-hazard" — those spoken of being God's already, before conversion. Calvin agrees, grounding it in the book of life and adding that "many sheep wander without the flock for a time" (John 17:6). Clarke shifts the ground: they are people "who have not resisted my Spirit, and consequently are now under its teachings", ready when the gospel reaches them. Wesley is briefest and least committed — "so he prophetically calls them that afterward believed." Robertson accepts the election language but conditions the outcome: they are "not yet saved, but who will be if Paul holds on" — the standing problem of every pastor. Ellicott declines the dogmatics and hears Elijah's seven thousand.

Barnes adds a comparison that stings: there may be more hope among the dissolute than among the self-satisfied, for "Paul had little success in philosophic Athens; he had great success in dissolute Corinth." No city's wickedness, he concludes, is a reason to despair of it.

Eighteen months follows, itself remarkable. Gill notes it was longer than Paul stayed anywhere except Ephesus, which he puts at two years — Barnes says three — Rome being confinement rather than choice. Clarke thinks both Thessalonian letters were written here, and that some place Galatians here too. Ellicott uses the span to explain the reach: it allowed not only a church in the city but work in the district around it, at Cenchrea with its deaconess (Romans 16:1) and further into Achaia.
12:
Gallio arrives with a reputation attached. Born M. Annaeus Novatus, he took the name on adoption by a rhetorician, and was brother to Seneca and uncle to Lucan — a Spanish family, Robertson notes. Seneca's praise is quoted by nearly everyone: no mortal was ever so pleasant to one man as Gallio was to all, his goodness carrying "no semblance of art or dissimulation". Statius calls him simply the sweet Gallio. Gill supplies the one glimpse of him off duty — catching a fever in Achaia, he went straight aboard ship "crying, that it was not the disease of the body, but of the place". Clarke supplies the end: Nero put all three brothers to death.

Robertson alone can date the scene, and knows it is a coup. A limestone inscription from the quarries near Delphi, a letter of Claudius, names Gallio proconsul of Achaia in the emperor's twenty-sixth acclamation, fixing Paul at Corinth in A.D. 50 and 51, or 51 and 52. The older voices had no such anchor. His conclusion is a manifesto: "It is amazing how Luke is confirmed whenever a new discovery is made."

The title itself is part of the confirmation. Ellicott credits Luke with "his characteristic accuracy in the use of official titles", since deputy means proconsul, which Achaia's governor was only after the province passed from the emperor back to the senate. On when that happened they disagree quietly — Ellicott dates the restoration to the year of the expulsion from Rome, Robertson to A.D. 44.

Why the Jews moved after eighteen quiet months is answered by motive, not evidence. Calvin offers two: a new deputy emboldened them, "as froward men use to abuse new things that they may procure some tumult", or they expected him to take their side. Robertson guesses similarly — they had heard of Gallio's moderation and thought a fresh proconsul a good chance, as they had rushed the praetors at Philippi.

Both verb and noun get corrected. Robertson finds a double compound "found nowhere else" and renders it a dash at Paul, "as if they would stand it no longer"; Ellicott objects to "insurrection", the word now meaning subjects revolting against rulers, and prefers "rushed upon". Ellicott adds the staging: governors heard grievances in the marketplace on fixed days, so the Jews, having "probably preconcerted their plans", waited for the court to sit.

Which law Paul was accused of breaking splits the corpus. Ellicott is certain it must be Rome's: Judaism was a licensed religion, and the charge was that Paul preached a new one that was not. Calvin is equally certain of the opposite, calling the Roman reading "cold" and "forced" and taking the charge to be innovation against the law of God. Barnes and Clarke decline to choose and read both, Clarke putting the argument in the accusers' mouths — "he is not a Jew, for he does not admit of circumcision; he is not a Gentile, for he preaches against the worship of the gods." Robertson concedes "the phrase has a double meaning" but insists Jewish law had no standing before Gallio, and that whatever was meant, no evidence for it was produced.

Two political conclusions pull against each other. Henry uses the toleration Rome granted the Jews to expose the charge: does permission to keep their own law include a right to impose it? "Must those therefore be prosecuted as criminals who worship God in any other way?" Calvin draws the reverse lesson. Rome forbade its magistrates to meddle in provincial religion only because it had no truth of its own to defend, and "nothing is more absurd than to leave the worship of God to men's choice" (Deuteronomy 17:18). Wesley, admiring Gallio's temper as much as anyone, ends with the reservation the others leave unsaid: "Yet one thing he lacked! But he knew it not and had no concern about it."
14:
Paul never gets to speak. Ellicott notes that the phrase about opening his mouth always signals the start of a set discourse — a formal apologia was coming, and "this, however, proved to be unnecessary." Robertson is blunter: "Before Paul could speak, Gallio cut in and ended the whole matter. According to their own statement Paul needed no defence."

Gallio's two categories of crime get translated four ways. The first word is straightforward wrong or injustice. The second is not. Barnes makes it the act of a practised hand — "him who is skilled, facile, or an adept in iniquity", the deed of a veteran offender — and notes it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Clarke renders it "destructive mischief". Ellicott wants "crime or fraud", objecting that "lewdness" now suggests one class of sin only, and pairs the terms forensically: open wrong such as robbery or assault, against wrong in which cunning is chief. Robertson keeps the etymology visible — one who does a thing easily and adroitly, "a slick citizen".

The concession Gallio offers is grammatically hollow. Robertson identifies the condition as the kind determined as unfulfilled: "the Jews had no case against Paul in a Roman court", and the sentence concedes nothing. Ellicott hears the same thing as tone rather than syntax: "the very turn of the phrase expresses an intense impatience. Even in the case supposed, his tolerance would have required an effort."

What the Jews brought instead was, in Gallio's summary, words and names. Robertson calls the plural contemptuous — Knowling's "a parcel of questions" — meaning talk, not deeds. The name in question is whether the teacher both sides call Jesus of Nazareth may also be called Christ. Ellicott catches the pronoun: your law means the law that affects you, and by it "the judge intimates that he sees through their appeal to law." Ellicott then draws the comparison that gives the scene its weight: Gallio refuses to become, as Pilate did after a weak protest, the executioner of an alien code.

On what to make of the ruling the voices split three ways, and the split is temperamental. Clarke makes Gallio a hero of conscience: "a better answer could not be given by man." The state, on this reading, has no right to control any man's religious opinion, and had every ruler acted so, the persecution laws that remain "blots and disgraces on the statute books of almost all the civilized nations of Europe" would be unwritten. Calvin refuses the compliment. He grants the nation was contentious and that Paul himself rebukes trifling over words (Titus 3:9), but "Gallio is not worthy to be excused who doth mock the holy law of God together with their curiosity", for "when the worship of God is in hand, the strife is not about words". Wesley sits between them, reading the manner rather than the doctrine — "he speaks with the utmost coolness and contempt" — then turns it on the reader: the question of the name of Jesus "is of more importance than all things else under heaven", and yet human reason, curious about everything, "abhors to inquire into it."

Robertson alone traces what the decision did. It established nothing in favour of Christianity; it merely left the movement a form of Judaism and so not against Roman law — which, he says, "opened the door for Paul's preaching all over the Roman Empire."

Whether anyone was struck at the clearing of the court is a bare factual disagreement. Barnes says the verb "does not denote that there was any violence"; Clarke agrees it was "simply an authoritative dismission"; Gill has them dismissed with a warning not to come back. Ellicott alone sees the lictors: the order was given to clear the court, "and the Jews, who did not immediately retreat were exposed to the ignominy of blows from their rods."
17:
Who did the beating is a textual question before a historical one. Gill and Barnes take the Greek bystanders at their word, Barnes reading the assault as pagan indignation at Jewish bigotry, though some copies read "Jews". Clarke turns the evidence the other way: "Greeks" is missing from the two oldest manuscripts, from the Coptic and Vulgate, and from two of the fathers, while three others read "Jews" — and "it is much more likely that the Jews beat one of their own rulers, through envy at his conversion". Ellicott agrees the word is an interpolation by someone who thought a synagogue ruler likelier struck by strangers than by his own people. Robertson assumes it: "violent hostile reaction against their leader who had failed so miserably", who "began to beat him, even if they could not beat Paul."

Whose man Sosthenes was follows from that. Clarke, Ellicott and Calvin have him already leaning to Paul — Calvin calls him one of Paul's companions and advocates — so the blows punish treachery. Wesley reads him the other way, "probably Paul's chief accuser", beaten by his own party for wasting their time. Gill and Robertson leave the conversion until later, Robertson noting drily that "the beating did Sosthenes good", since he ends a co-worker of the man he prosecuted (1 Corinthians 1:1).

Whether Gallio watched is unsettled. Barnes puts the assault as the court broke up; Clarke doubts he saw it at all; Wesley cannot believe it was in his sight, "though at no great distance from him". Ellicott and Calvin place it in front of him, the Jews having "not shrunk from giving vent to their rage even before the tribunal".

The last clause has damaged Gallio's name more than anything he did, and three voices rise to defend him. Barnes objects that he is "most improperly used to represent the indifferent, the worldly, the careless, and the skeptical", and denies any propriety in preaching from the verse against such men. Clarke calls the censure "manifest injustice": the magistrate had no business restraining the free teaching of conscience where the state was not endangered. Robertson is briskest: the words are "quite beside the mark" as a verdict on Gallio's religion — he "looked the other way with a blind eye" at a police-court matter, and shows up in Luke "as a clear headed judge who would not be led astray by Jewish subterfuges".

Ellicott grants the exegesis, then withholds the acquittal. Luke probably meant only that the proconsul disregarded the clamour, and laissez faire would be motto enough. "The general impression, however, as to his character is not without its truth." He supplies the sequel the defenders omit: the same easy gentleness left Gallio unfit to resist Nero's court, he returned to Rome and shared in ministering to the emperor's vices, and ended under the tyrant's displeasure — killed, or a suicide, or, in Tacitus, begging Nero for his life.

Calvin prosecutes. The indifference was contempt for the religion, not sluggishness: Rome licensed vows to every idol of Asia and Greece, yet sacrifice to the God of Israel was a capital matter, so "in the common liberty of all manner of superstition, only true religion was excepted". Gallio winked, wanting the Jews to destroy each other and their worship with them. And the verdict is not his own — "by the mouth of Luke, the Spirit condemneth Gallio's carelessness, because he did not aid a man who was unjustly punished." Magistrates who reach no hand to the oppressed "are fans to kindle boldness to do hurt".

The two readings cannot both stand. For Robertson, Sosthenes "richly deserved" what he got; for Calvin he is guiltless, and failing to protect him is the sin of the passage. Clarke sees only what the blows prove: recourse to "manual logic, which was an indisputable proof of the badness of their own cause."
18:
Paul stays on, and Calvin thinks the reversal significant. Elsewhere he fled the moment persecution rose, since his presence drew the rage down on the church; here, seeing their malice bridled, "he had rather sting and nettle them, than by departing minister unto them any new occasion of rage." Clarke supplies the legal reason: after Gallio's ruling no state persecution was possible, and citizenship made Paul's person "sacred as long as he did nothing contrary to the laws". Robertson agrees there was "no reason for haste in leaving".

Then the chapter's hardest sentence: who was shorn? The Greek permits either man. Clarke sets out the roll-call — Chrysostom, Grotius, Erasmus and Wesley for Aquila; Jerome, Augustine and Bede for Paul — concludes "the bare letter of the text determines nothing", then leans to Paul anyway. Wesley prints it as Aquila's; Barnes says the connection "evidently requires us to understand it of Paul", the Vulgate reading Aquila and the Syriac Paul. The Ethiopic and two Latin versions solved it by making the verb plural and shaving both.

The arguments run on different tracks. Ellicott has "hardly the shadow of a doubt" for Paul: a vow would have obliged Aquila to go to Jerusalem rather than stay at Ephesus, and James later speaks as though Paul's readiness to join such vows were already known (Acts 21:23). Robertson argues from word order and gender — the participle cannot be Priscilla's, and though Aquila stands nearest, the neighbouring participles are Paul's. Calvin will not fight: "neither skilleth it much," though he too reads Paul. Henry sees no harm either way, noting that some throw it on Aquila as a Jew who "retained perhaps more of his Judaism than was convenient".

What kind of vow is as open. Ellicott is confident it was the temporary Nazarite of Numbers 6:2 — no wine, no razor, the hair burnt at last on the altar. Barnes supposes Paul, being outside Palestine, cut his hair where he was and completed the rite at Jerusalem. Robertson rejects the identification — "it was not a Nazarite vow which could be absolved only in Jerusalem" — and ends in candour: "it is not clear what sort of a vow Paul had taken nor why he took it." Chrysostom noticed the defect from the other end: shearing the head with a vow was the Jewish custom, "but then there ought to be also a sacrifice, which was not the case here."

Ellicott's solution to the awkwardness is the neatest thing here. A Nazarite grows his hair, so cropping looks like the reverse of the vow — but the word is shorn, not shaved, and cutting during the term was permitted. The clippings still had to reach the Temple, which is why, on his reading, Paul was so set on keeping the coming feast.

For motive Ellicott offers thankfulness after fear, pointing to the vision and the deliverance, and the principle of being all things to all men (1 Corinthians 9:20) — a vow testifying to his own people that he neither despised the Law nor taught others to. Barnes reaches the same motive, then withdraws: "where nothing is recorded, conjecture is useless."

Calvin's reading is sharpest. Paul cannot have vowed for his own sake; it would be absurd "for him to bind his own conscience with that religion from which he had loosed all other men". He shore his head only to accommodate Jews not yet taught; against the charge of play-acting, "as touching the substance of purifying he did not dissemble". Then the target: Rome fetches vows out of this passage, but "Paul was moved with no religion to make his vow", and there is all the difference between tolerating an old rite until it dies out and reviving a dead one. Chrysostom sees only the direction of travel: "See how the Law was breaking up."
19:
Ephesus draws out the antiquarians. Gill runs through its discarded names — Alopes, Ortygia, Smyrna Trachea — and the rival founders, Amazons or Ephesus son of Caystrus. Ellicott sets it under Croesus and the Artemis temple, and names what made it dangerous: East and West met there, so Greek religion turned Oriental, "fruitful in magic, and mysteries, and charms". Barnes and Clarke both quote the same traveller, Chandler, on the Greek peasants "inhabiting the wreck of their greatness", living in the vaults of the stadium and the tombs of their ancestors. Clarke reads on — goats driven in for shade, crows insulting the silence, a partridge calling in the theatre — and ends on the seven churches: "the Church of Ephesus is blotted out of the map of Christianity! Be silent and adore."

Whether Paul arrived alone turns on one letter. Ellicott notes the better copies read "they came", and Gill finds the plural in the Syriac. Robertson explains it as Luke mentioning the departure by anticipation. On why the couple stayed, Ellicott thinks Paul had stopped working at the trade and left them to it; Chrysostom gives the purpose directly — he left them "that they should teach" — and pauses over who is named first: "lo, a woman also".

The invitation to remain is the one Paul refuses, and it puzzles his readers. Ellicott takes the request as the earnest of what followed, since nowhere else did Paul find such receptivity: Corinth got milk, Ephesus "the whole counsel of God". Calvin finds the refusal strange for that reason: heard more patiently here than anywhere, and asked to stay, he would not — so "we may easily gather that he had some great cause to go up to Jerusalem in haste."

The reason given may not be Luke's. Clarke reports the whole clause about keeping the feast missing from the oldest manuscripts and four versions, Griesbach flagging it doubtful and White judging it probably to be struck out; Robertson agrees it is absent from the best copies and guesses it was added to explain the "going up" of the next verse. Those who keep it cannot agree which feast it was: Barnes and Clarke say the passover, Ellicott argues for Pentecost on practical grounds — miss it and nothing falls before Tabernacles, by which time autumn sailing is dangerous — and Robertson, doubting the clause, still thinks Pentecost the likely destination. Wesley heads off the inference: Paul went not from any conscience that he was bound to keep Jewish feasts, but to reach many countrymen at once.

"If God will" gets more attention than four words suggest. Ellicott makes it another point of contact with James (James 4:15), meaning more to them than the formula usually does "in the lips of Christians". Robertson is content that Jews, Greeks and Romans all said such things, then and now: "it is simply a recognition that we are in God's hands."

Where he went up is not stated. Robertson builds the case for Jerusalem from three details — up is the standing idiom for that city, down to Antioch suits leaving Jerusalem rather than Caesarea, and no errand at Caesarea suggests itself. Clarke agrees, offering the same homely analogy that all England is spoken of as below London. On which congregation was saluted, Clarke and Wesley agree on Jerusalem, "the Mother, or Apostolic Church" — from which, Clarke adds pointedly, even Rome was only a daughter.

Ellicott thinks the verse conceals much: perhaps one of the three shipwrecks, Philip the Evangelist at Caesarea, the vow completed in the Temple, then at Antioch the confrontation with Peter of Galatians 2:11, the Judaising party having gathered strength in Paul's absence. Robertson knows that placement and prefers an earlier. Both see what follows: Paul sets out on a third tour with neither Barnabas nor Silas, having come back from the second alone.
24:
Calvin reads the timing as providence: Paul is forced from Ephesus, and "Apollos cometh in his place to supply his absence." How he began matters, since he became Paul's successor at Corinth and half of a famous sentence — "I have planted, Apollos hath watered" (1 Corinthians 3:6). Henry says the narrative leaves Paul travelling and turns aside here because without it parts of Paul's letters cannot be understood.

The name provokes an argument. Henry insists it "was not Apollo, the name of one of the heathen gods, but Apollos", and suggests it may be the Apelles of Romans 16:10. Clarke takes the opposite line, finds it strange a Jew should bear a false god's name, and conjectures the parents were Gentiles who came over to Judaism after the boy was named. Ellicott and Robertson defuse it: the name contracts Apollonius, and Codex Bezae reads the longer form.

Alexandria explains him. Robertson notes the Jews were a third of the population, with a great university and library, and that Jewish-Alexandrian philosophy grew there under Philo, "who was still living". Clarke wanders from the Pharos to Bonaparte's capture of the city in 1798.

Ellicott turns his note into an essay, the boldest claim in the chapter. Luther, struck by the Alexandrian cast of Hebrews and the mystery of its authorship that made Origen say God alone knew who wrote it, guessed Apollos; later critics strengthened the guess by parallels with Philo. Ellicott adds a step of his own: the Wisdom of Solomon is likewise anonymous and likewise ascribed to Philo, and its agreement with Hebrews in style and language is so close "that it is scarcely possible to resist the inference that they must have come from the same pen", representing "different stages in the spiritual growth of the same man" — Apollos. Even without conceding that, an Alexandrian Jew arriving now could hardly have escaped Philo, and to Apollos may be traced the idea that the unseen Godhead shows itself in the Logos.

What the word behind "eloquent" means is unsettled, since the Greek covers both speech and thought. Robertson lays out the fork — a man of words or a man of ideas — and concludes Apollos was both. Ellicott says it "implies learning as well as eloquence", used above all of historians. Henry collects the renderings: a prudent man, a learned man, a good historian, one who could speak well, "an oracle of a man".

Whether eloquence is fit in a minister at all is Calvin's question, answered with unusual balance. Paul denies the kingdom consists in words and was not himself commended for speaking: "the Lord would have the chief apostle to want this virtue, that the power of the Spirit might appear more excellent in his rude and homely speech." But Paul's want of utterance "did no whit let but that the Lord might choose to himself eloquent ministers"; the gift is dangerous only where boasting is sought. Wesley states the rule in one line: "Every talent may be of use in the kingdom of God, if joined with the knowledge of the Scriptures and fervour of spirit."

On being mighty in the Scriptures three notes converge from different directions. Henry draws the distinction: many could quote texts off-hand and had only "the form of knowledge, and the letter of the law", whereas Apollos "understood the sense and meaning of them", so that "a convincing, commanding, confirming power went along with all his expositions". Calvin says the same, then withholds the credit from the man: the force belongs to Scripture, "that it hath sufficient force both to defend the truth, and also to refute the subtilty of Satan." Robertson turns the phrase on the profession — "there is no excuse for ignorance of the Scriptures on the part of preachers" — recalling that his teacher John Broadus made this verse his last lecture.
25:
The verb behind "instructed" later gave the Church its catechumens, as Ellicott notes; Robertson digs at the root — to re-sound, to re-echo, "to teach by repeated dinning into the ears". Gill guesses the teachers were parents once John's disciples, who moved from Judea to Alexandria. Ellicott concludes the Baptist's influence reached further than the Gospels record, to Alexandria and its ascetic communities.

What Apollos lacked is answered three incompatible ways. Ellicott says he knew the life, death and resurrection and accepted Jesus as Christ, but was taught by someone who never passed the Baptist's standpoint, so "the Christ was for him the head of a glorified Judaism, retaining all its distinctive features" — he had not learnt that circumcision was nothing. Barnes says the opposite: "it is clear that he had not heard that Jesus was the Messiah." He had the right expectation of a humble and suffering deliverer, and was ready for the news. Robertson takes a middle line: Apollos knew what the Baptist knew at his death — including that Jesus was the Son of God — but not the Cross, the Resurrection or Pentecost. He taught accurately, Robertson adds, what he knew — and Clarke, resisting a proposed negative in the text, agrees: "surely it is possible for a man to teach accurately what he knows."

Whose spirit was fervent divides two careful readers. Ellicott is certain the noun means the man's own spirit, "not the Holy Spirit of God", citing Romans 12:11; Calvin is as certain the other way, since Luke "doth attribute zeal to the Spirit". Robertson keeps only the image: the word means boiling, like water or yeast.

Calvin makes zeal and knowledge the lesson. "Doctrine without zeal is either like a sword in the hand of a madman, or else it lieth still as cold and without use" — but knowledge must come first and govern it, since "many are fervent without consideration". Then the rebuke: if a man not fully taught preached so diligently, what excuse have those who know more and do less? He also takes "the baptism of John" as covering the Baptist's whole ministry, and draws a rule from it: it is "wickedness and impious profanation to pull" sacraments "away from doctrine".

Then the remembered scene. Ellicott notes the best manuscripts put Priscilla's name first and infers a woman of more than ordinary culture, "able, with a prophetic insight, to help even the disciple of Philo" to read the Scriptures better. Clarke presses the moral on his male readers: a public teacher, eloquent and mighty in the Scriptures, "was not ashamed to be indebted to the instructions of a Christian woman". Robertson admires the manner: instead of abusing a brilliant young preacher for what he did not know, they took him home and filled the gaps, "a needed and delicate task".

Calvin gives with one hand and withdraws with the other. He praises the couple's freedom from envy, teaching privately what Apollos would say publicly, so "they keep silence, and he alone is heard"; he praises Apollos for being taught "not only by an handy-craftsman, but also by a woman"; and he turns it against Rome — women were not then so ignorant of the word as the Papists would have them, since "one of the chief teachers of the Church was instructed by a woman". Then the qualification: Priscilla did this "at home in her own house, that she might not overthrow the order prescribed by God and nature".

Whether Apollos was baptised again is left contradictory. Ellicott thinks it follows "almost necessarily", by the parallel of the disciples in the next chapter. Robertson denies it in a sentence: "He was not rebaptized, but only received fuller information." Chrysostom, who noticed the problem first, could not settle it — the text records no baptism, yet "it is likely that he did in fact receive baptism."
27:
Luke does not say why Apollos wanted Achaia; Codex Bezae answers. Clarke translates the addition: certain Corinthians staying at Ephesus heard him and "entreated him to pass over with them to their own country", after which the Ephesians wrote ahead. Gill reports the same reading, and Robertson thinks it plausible: "preachers often receive calls because visitors from other places hear them."

The letter has a long afterlife. Ellicott calls it "the first instance of what were afterwards known technically as letters of commendation", then makes it sting: the Corinthian partisans later held these letters up as a point in which Apollos excelled Paul, and Paul answered that he needed no such epistle, the church he planted being itself an epistle "known and read of all men" (2 Corinthians 3:3). Robertson traces the same line to the same verse. Calvin reads the letter more widely: it asked the Corinthians not merely to lodge the man but "that they should suffer him to teach", lest the gifts given for edifying "lie buried".

"Through grace" attaches to either verb. Barnes and Clarke find either possible, the translators taking the obvious one and tying it to believing; Ellicott and Calvin attach it to helping; Robertson refuses to choose — "both are true as the references show." Wesley states the principle instead: "it is through grace only that any gift of any one is profitable to another."

What Apollos left at Corinth was a party. Clarke calls him "the innocent cause of a sort of schism", some preferring him to every other teacher. Barnes notes the divisions, then draws the better point: Paul kept his confidence and affection throughout, showing "that great success by one minister need not excite the envy" of another. Ellicott identifies the faction — philosophising Jews and proselytes, against the narrower circumcision party round Cephas — and insists "not a word escapes from St. Paul that indicates any doctrinal difference between himself and Apollos".

Ellicott then says what the others would not. Apollos reached Paul's conclusion by another route — the argument of Hebrews rather than Galatians, hearers treated as men pressing to maturity rather than children fed with milk — and this gave him "a larger measure of real or apparent success in dealing with the Jews than had attended the labours of St. Paul". Wesley reaches a narrower version: Apollos "was better able to convince the Jews, than to convert the heathens", and watered where Paul planted.

Whether he convinced anyone is a dispute about a tense. Gill has the Jews "refuted over and over, and confounded to the last degree"; Barnes says he "bore down all opposition, and effectually silenced them"; Clarke has him vehemently confuting them. Robertson takes the rare double compound — to argue an opponent down to a finish — notes it stands in the imperfect, and concludes it "does not mean that Apollos convinced these rabbis, but he had the last word". Scripture was the right weapon, he adds, because the rabbis knew the oral law better than the written.

Calvin builds a doctrine of Scripture on that. If the law and the prophets had light enough for Apollos to prove Jesus is the Christ "as if he did point out the matter with his finger", the gospel added to them must make that knowledge plainer still — so it is "detestable blasphemy" to call Scripture dark and doubtful, and the refusal to dispute out of Scripture stands refuted by Luke, since nothing was more stubborn than the Jews and these were the weapons that beat them. Ellicott closes the story where the record does: back at Ephesus, reluctant to return to Corinth lest he seem the occasion of schism, last seen with Zenas the lawyer (Titus 3:13). Robertson adds the guess that will not die, holding it loosely: some think Apollos wrote Hebrews, "a guess that may be correct".
